title: Molecular Representations for Machine Learning-Based Environmental Pollutant Prediction: Applications and Critical As-assessment
content: Machine learning is widely used to predict the environmental behavior and effects of pollutants. Molecular representation strongly influences these predictions, yet its suitability varies with the endpoint and the available data. This review examines how descriptors, fingerprints, SMILES strings, molecular graphs, and pretrained models evolved and were applied to physicochemical properties and environmental fate, bioaccumulation and bioconcentration, and ecotoxicity. Which representation suits a task therefore follows from what information the endpoint requires, not from how recent the method is. Conventional descriptors and fingerprints remain competitive for endpoints governed by size, polarity, or specific functional groups, and graph-based and pretrained models have not consistently outperformed them. Where endpoints also depend on uptake, exposure, or organism characteristics, contextual variables can matter as much as the encoding itself. Direct comparisons under identical conditions remain few, and reported performance is rarely comparable across studies because datasets, algorithms, validation procedures, and chemical coverage differ. Representation choice should therefore be reported with the data conditions under which it was evaluated. Claims of improvement should rest on external validation and an explicit applicability-domain analysis, so that model predictions can support screening and risk assessment.
